levels.label: Nudge
levels.text: Which code sees every refusal? Which code sees the success? You need an entry from both, and exactly one entry per call.

levels.label: Approach
levels.text:
`audit(entry)` lives in src/lib/audit.js: read its header comment. Write the entry when the outcome is known, with the fields from the card. When nobody could be identified (a bad token), `sub` is null, because you must not take identity from a token you could not verify.

But a token that verified and was refused only for its scope is a known caller: the entry should say who tried. Think about which code has verified the token on a call it refuses.

levels.label: Near-solution
levels.text:
The scope gate sees the 401s and the 403s, so it can call `audit` just before it answers. The tool handler sees the success, so it records the allowed call.

The entry must never contain the token or customer data (a name, a balance). `npm run state` shows exactly what you wrote.

reveal.referenceBrief:
CONTEXT: Every privileged tool call must leave a record that lets someone reconstruct an incident. audit(entry) in src/lib/audit.js keeps entries in memory and /_lab/state (npm run state) shows them.

TASK: Record every call to POST /tools/freeze_card, allowed or denied, including calls with a bad or missing token, exactly once.

ACCEPTANCE: Each entry has: event "tool_call", action, outcome ("allowed" or "denied"), reason (on a denial, for example invalid_token or insufficient_scope), sub (the person the agent acts for, taken only from a verified token: null when the token failed verification or there was none, but a token that verified and was refused for its scope is still a known caller, so record who tried), actor (act.sub, or null), allowedActions (the array from the token, or []), accountId (null if there was none) and requestId (req.id). Never put the token, or customer data such as a name or balance, in an entry.

VERIFY: npm run step -- 7, then npm run state to read a sample.
reveal.approach:
One entry per call, written once the decision is made. Denials count as much as successes: a run of failures is what probing looks like.

Identity comes only from claims that were verified. A bad token yields sub: null, not whatever the unverified payload claims.
commonMistakes: Writing an "allowed" entry before the handler runs. Milestone 8 adds a refusal inside the handler, and you would log the same call twice.
Taking sub from jwt.decode on a token that failed verification.
Recording a scope refusal with sub: null, because the code that writes the entry never saw the verified claims.
Logging the Authorization header, or the token, for debugging.
Logging the account holder's name or balance "for context".
Forgetting the requests with no token at all.
